PeerJ - Response to Reviewers 
Manuscript: #8885

High nonpublication rate from publication professionals 
hinders evidence-based publication practices


Reviewers’ Comments
Authors’ Responses
Reviewer 1: Ksenija Bazdaric
Suggest title change to be more specific ie, include “the International Society for Medical Publication Professionals experience”.
Thank you for this suggestion.  We would prefer to keep the title concise and avoid the risk of readers inferring the article came from International Society for Medical Publication Professionals (ISMPP).  We have, however, included more specific details about ISMPP in the introduction and the abstract specifies that the data came from the ISMPP Annual Meetings. 

Introduction – add more information about ISMPP, its mission, and members.
We have added the following information to the Introduction:

The International Society for Medical Publications Professionals (ISMPP), a not-for-profit association with > 1,400 members, has a mission to “advance the medical publication profession globally through enhanced integrity and transparency in medical publications, improved standards and best practices, and education, advocacy, and professional collaborations” (http://www.ismpp.org/mission-and-vision).

Results – explain Figure 1 in the text; describe the characteristics of the posters in a table.
We had provided the absolute and relative publication rate in the text in the Results and included the following text in the figure legend “Figure 1. Low publication rates from publication professionals versus medical research community. Abbreviation: ISMPP, International Society for Medical Publication Professionals.”  However, we have modified the description of Figure 1 and added a new table (Table 1). The data in Table 1 were included in the original Supplementary file, but we have now provided the results to the reader in the main paper.  We have also expanded our discussion of the implications of this result in the Discussion (see below).  

 
Of the 220 abstracts submitted to ISMPP Annual Meetings, 185 (84.1%) were accepted for presentation; of these, 164 (88.6%) were published in CMRO.   Almost all of the research presented at ISMPP was never published in full in peer-reviewed journals; the publication rate was 2.4% (4/164; Fig. 1).  Of the 4 research abstracts subsequently published as full papers, only 1 had been selected by ISMPP for an oral presentation (Table 1). 
Provide more information about the authors of the abstracts – where do they work, are they working as freelancers for a company or a journal?
We have added additional information about the authors (inserted after reference to Table 1):

“…for an oral presentation (Table 1).  The four publications were authored by 11 individuals who had advanced degrees (PhD or medical degree). Of these 11, eight were also Certified Medical Publication Professionals, signifying that they had passed an international exam on publication ethics and practices.  All the authors worked as publication professional employees in medical communication or biopharmaceutical companies and, on average, had 20 peer-reviewed publications each. 

Provide more information about the 4 published abstracts – what are they about, are the corresponding authors active in publishing, do they have a publication record?
We have provided the titles of the published abstracts in Table 1.  We have added further information about the authors (see response to comment 4)
Provide more information about the low publication rate, even speculation on why publication professionals don’t publish and some practical implications.
We have expanded the Discussion, which now includes more information (including speculation) on why publication professionals have such a low publication rate. 

“Our study has quantified, for the first time, the extent of nonpublication by publication professionals.  Additional studies, ideally with qualitative research methods, will be required to investigate the reasons for the low publication rate.  We speculate that lack of time may be one of the main drivers for nonpublication.  A systematic review, which investigated the reasons why biomedical researchers don’t publish, reported that lack of time was the most frequent, as well as the most important, reason provided for nonpublication (Scherer et al., 2015).  In our experience, most publication professionals are not employed to design, conduct, and publish research on publication practices.  Such research is likely to depend on considerable “after hours” time.   Additional reasons may include lack of resources (eg, limited funding to gain expert support from statisticians and professional medical writers), competing priorities (eg, professional duties, personal responsibilities), and uncertainty regarding the most important and feasible research projects to pursue. We also recognize that publication professionals may conduct the type of research (eg, surveys and descriptive analyses on operational issues) that may not be appropriate nor robust enough for the peer-reviewed literature.”  

Methods are well described
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Conclusions are appropriately stated, connected with the original questions, and the limitations are explained.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Annotations in pdf of manuscript.
We have reviewed the comments in the .pdf version of the manuscript.  Minor editorial changes have been made. 


Reviewer 2: Joan Marsh
Manuscript is well written
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Figure 1 could be omitted.
We would prefer to keep this single figure as it provides a strong visual message directly related to the primary outcome of our study and also includes comparative data (ie, publication rates of other conferences) that provide context for the Discussion.
Provide more information on the example of topics covered at ISMPP – perhaps the four selected for oral presentation and/or the four that were published.
As per our response to a comment from Reviewer 1, we have now included a new table (Table 1) that describes the topics of the 4 research abstracts subsequently published as full papers.
Two sentences in the Introduction could be removed (difficulty in publishing, 39% of research from peer review congresses not published)
We would prefer to retain these sentences as they reinforce the difficulty that others (eg, editors) have faced in trying to conduct and publish research on publication practices.
In the introduction, the authors stage that 39% of presentations at peer review congresses have not been published (no date range given), but in the figure and the discussion they give 60.5% citing the same reference.
In the introduction, we provide a direct quote from the Malički paper and that is why we used 39%.  This 39% refers to the NONpublication rate from the Peer Review Congress.  For the figure, we used the actual data from the Malički paper and present the publication rate of 60.5% (ie, 39 + 60.5 = 99.5%).  The Malički paper can provide the reader with details on the Peer Review Congresses (number, location, abstracts presented, corresponding papers published etc…), but we have now modified the description of this study in the Introduction to include the date range.

“Malički and colleagues reported that “…39% of research presented at Peer Review and Biomedical Publication (PRC) congresses had not been fully published…”, based on an analysis of the seven congresses from 1989 to 2013 (Malički, von Elm & Marušic, 2014).”
Would be helpful to know the percentage of abstracts selected for an oral presentation
In the Results, we provide the percentage of abstracts selected for posters (133/164; 81.1%).  The remaining abstracts were, therefore, selected for oral presentations (ie, 31/164; 18.9%).  We have added this additional sentence to the Results.

“The remaining abstracts were selected for oral presentations (ie, 31/164; 18.9%).”  

Research question was clearly stated and the investigation was well conducted.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
The exact date of the MEDLINE search should be given.
We provided the month and year, but have added the date of the last MEDLINE search (ie, 17 December 2014). 
The findings appear valid.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
A well written paper.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.


Reviewer 3: Paola De Castro
The manuscript is well written and the arguments are clearly explained.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Provide more information about ISMPP and how it relates to similar associations.
As per our response to a comment from Reviewer 1, we have added more details about ISMPP in the Introduction.  Similar to other professional associations, it is a not-for-profit organisation.
Study is limited by relying on one source ie, ISMPP and only checking for publications in MEDLINE.  Authors should explain why they searched only MEDLINE and not other databases.
We have expanded the limitations section of the Discussion to address this feedback and your additional comment (#8):

“Our study has limitations, including a focus on ISMPP Annual Meetings. As our intent was to investigate how well publication professionals contribute to the evidence base affecting publication practices, we focused on the largest annual meeting for publication professionals.  We recognize that publication professionals may attend other meetings, but these meetings may not be focused primarily on publication practices, may not have dedicated sessions for research-based presentations from publication professionals, and may not have been held as consistently or for as long as the ISMPP has held annual meetings.  Our study is also limited by the focus on peer-reviewed publications included in the MEDLINE database (up until December 2014).  We recognize that peer-reviewed publications may have appeared in other databases and after we conducted our search.  We focused on MEDLINE because it was readily accessible and is one of the largest databases for medical research articles.  We reasoned that those with an interest in medical research publication practices would search MEDLINE for relevant peer-reviewed articles.”
The structure conforms to an acceptable format. The supplementary material is useful.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
The text is subdivided in coherent sections.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Better describe Figure 1 and improve its caption.
We have revised the caption for Figure 1:

“Figure 1. Low publication rates from ISMPP Annual Meetings versus publication rates from biomedical conferences (Scherer et al., 2015) and Peer Review Congresses (Malički, von Elm & Marušic, 2014). Abbreviation: ISMPP, International Society for Medical Publication Professionals.”

Research question is clearly defined and the methods described with sufficient information to be reproducible.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Some abstracts may have been published after December 2014; this should be mentioned as well as the fact that other peer-reviewed articles may not be included in MEDLINE.
As per our response to your comment (#3), we have expanded the limitations section of the Discussion to address this feedback.
 
Data are correct; supplementary material is useful. 
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
Conclusions are connected with the original question and consistent with the title of the article.
We thank the peer reviewer for this positive feedback.
